paragraphs.heading: Corals turning white
paragraphs.text: Coral bleaching is when corals go white because they lose the algae they live in partnership with, along with the pigments used for photosynthesis. Changes in water temperature, light, saltiness or nutrients can all set it off. A bleached coral is under stress, more likely to starve or fall ill, and at risk of dying.

paragraphs.heading: A partnership under strain
paragraphs.text: Reef corals depend on zooxanthellae, single-celled organisms that live inside coral tissue and give it its colour. Using photosynthesis, they supply the coral with nutrients, which matters a great deal in clear tropical water that is poor in nutrients. In return, the coral gives them the carbon dioxide and ammonium they need. These partners can meet up to 90 percent of a coral's energy needs.

paragraphs.heading: How bleaching happens
paragraphs.text: Unusually warm or cool water, strong light and even some microbial diseases can break the partnership down. To survive in the short term, the coral polyp eats or expels its zooxanthellae, and it turns pale or fully white. Under mild stress some corals turn bright blue, pink, purple or yellow instead, because their own pigments stay or increase. Without its partners the coral may begin to starve, and the longer the bad conditions last, the lower its chances.

paragraphs.heading: Recovery or collapse
paragraphs.text: To recover, zooxanthellae have to move back into the coral's tissue and start photosynthesizing again. If the polyps starve to death instead, they decay and leave behind their calcium carbonate skeletons. Algae then take over those skeletons and stop new coral from growing. Over time the skeletons erode and the reef falls apart.

paragraphs.heading: Warming seas
paragraphs.text: The leading cause is rising ocean temperature driven by climate change. Local triggers cause local bleaching, but the large-scale events of recent years have been set off by global warming. Marine heatwaves caused by El Niño are among the main causes of widespread bleaching and coral death. In 2022 the IPCC reported that mass bleaching had become sharply more frequent and severe worldwide since the early 1980s.

paragraphs.heading: Recent events
paragraphs.text: The Great Barrier Reef had its first major bleaching in 1998, and three events followed between 2016 and 2020. In 2016 alone, bleaching killed 29 to 50 percent of that reef's coral. In April 2024, NOAA confirmed that the world was in its fourth and largest global bleaching event. From January 2023 to September 2025, bleaching-level heat reached about 84.4% of the world's reef area, and bleaching was recorded in at least 83 countries and territories.
